1.1.1.architect: SPACE operates in the domain of software specification engineering augmented by LLM capabilities, sitting at the intersection of three well-established fields: requirements engineering, prompt engineering, and developer tooling. The architectural significance is that it treats specification creation as a structured data flow problem rather than a free-form documentation task. The dependency graph between the 7 series (Domain & Audience, Assumptions & Abstraction, etc.) follows a directed acyclic graph pattern where each series produces artifacts consumed by downstream series. This is architecturally analogous to a build system like Webpack where modules declare their dependencies. The core concern is converting unstructured human knowledge into structured, machine-readable specifications — a transformation problem that requires careful interface design between the elicitation layer (questions), the synthesis layer (artifact extraction), and the export layer (multi-format generation). The separation between FrameworkDefinition (the static 326-question schema) and SessionState (the runtime answer accumulator) follows the Command-Query Separation pattern, keeping the question structure immutable while session data mutates freely.
1.1.1.practitioner: SPACE's domain maps directly to the src/ directory structure: src/engine/ handles the specification pipeline, src/storage/ persists session state, src/llm/ integrates providers for refinement and synthesis, src/export/ generates multi-format output, and web/ provides the browser interface. The 326 probes live in JSON framework definition files loaded by src/data/framework-loader.ts. When implementing new features, the practitioner needs to understand that Series 1 answers seed the artifact dictionary, which Series 2 reads to scope entity modeling, which Series 3 uses for relationship mapping — this is a pipeline where each stage's output becomes the next stage's input. The TypeScript types in src/types/index.ts define the contracts: FrameworkDefinition, SessionState, ArtifactDictionary. Any new feature must produce or consume artifacts that fit the ArtifactValue interface with its source_question_id, confidence, and derived_from fields. The 7 export formats in src/export/formatters/ each implement the same ExportResult interface, so adding a new format (like PDF) means implementing a single class that returns content, filename, mime_type, and size_bytes.
1.1.1.strategist: The primary domain — structured specification generation for software projects — is underserved by existing tools. Current alternatives include Notion templates (manual, no automation), Google Docs (free-form, no structure), and AI chatbots (no systematic coverage). SPACE differentiates by offering deterministic, reproducible specification workflows backed by a validated 326-probe framework. The target market is mid-stage startups (Series A-C) and enterprise innovation teams who spend 2-4 weeks on requirements gathering before each sprint cycle. The value proposition is reducing this to 2-4 hours of structured input followed by automated spec generation. The competitive moat is the framework itself — the 326 probes encode domain expertise that would take teams months to develop independently. The go-to-market strategy should target developer communities (HN, dev.to, GitHub) with the CLI tool as a free OSS entry point, then upsell the web UI and team collaboration features. Success metric: reduce time-to-specification by 80% while maintaining or improving spec quality scores.
1.1.1.critic: The domain classification is somewhat inflated. SPACE is fundamentally a structured questionnaire with artifact extraction and template-based export — calling it 'specification engineering' overstates the formal rigor. The 326 probes are pre-authored, not generated, so the 'automatic creation engine' moniker is misleading; it's more of a 'guided specification elicitation engine.' A skeptic would note that the LLM integration layer (src/llm/) adds significant complexity but unclear value — if the probes are well-designed, human answers should be sufficient without LLM refinement. The dependency graph between series, while elegant architecturally, creates a rigid workflow that may frustrate users who want to jump to specific sections. The sub-disciplines claimed (ontological modeling, JAD facilitation) are loosely borrowed; the system doesn't actually implement OWL-style reasoning or JAD's multi-stakeholder facilitation. The real risk is that the domain is too niche: developers who need specs usually just write them, and those who don't won't be motivated by a 326-question questionnaire regardless of how well-structured it is.

1.1.2.architect: The audience segmentation reveals distinct interface requirements that should influence the system's layering. Practitioners (TypeScript developers) interact with the CLI in src/cli/ and need programmatic access to artifacts. Product managers interact via the web UI in web/ and need visual progress tracking and export capabilities. Architects need the full artifact dictionary and dependency graph visualization. The baseline familiarity assumption — that users understand REST APIs, npm, and LLM concepts — directly constrains the error handling strategy in src/engine/validator.ts: validation errors should reference question IDs and artifact keys, not internal state representations. The audience profile also shapes the context_template field in OpenEndedQuestion: templates should assume knowledge of basic software engineering but explain SPACE-specific concepts like 'artifact dictionary' and 'series dependency' inline. The secondary audiences (maintainers, technical writers) consume exported artifacts, not the elicitation engine itself, which justifies the clean separation between src/engine/ (internal) and src/export/ (external consumption).
1.1.2.practitioner: The audience split determines implementation priorities. For CLI practitioners, the key files are src/cli/commands/run.ts (interactive questioning) and src/cli/commands/export.ts (output generation). The run command needs to handle the full session lifecycle: init → question display → answer collection → artifact extraction → progress tracking → next question routing. For the web audience, web/server.mjs serves the React frontend that needs to implement the same flow through a browser interface. The baseline familiarity with npm means we can use chalk, inquirer, and other CLI libraries without extensive onboarding docs. The TypeScript audience expects strong typing, so all public APIs in src/types/index.ts should be well-documented with JSDoc. The storage layer (src/storage/sqlite.ts and src/storage/filesystem.ts) should support both backends since practitioners may prefer SQLite for performance while maintainers may prefer filesystem for portability. Testing the audience assumption means verifying that the context_template on each question in the framework JSON files is sufficient for someone unfamiliar with SPACE terminology.
1.1.2.strategist: The practitioner-first audience strategy is correct for developer tool adoption — OSS CLI tools win when they're immediately useful without onboarding friction. However, the product manager secondary audience is underserved by the current architecture. PMs won't use a CLI; they need the web UI (web/) to be production-ready before any PM-facing marketing. The technical writer audience is the fastest path to viral adoption: if SPACE specs become the input format for documentation generators (Docusaurus, GitBook, ReadMe), each technical writer who adopts SPACE creates a multiplier effect. The roadmap should prioritize: (1) CLI for developers (MVP, months 1-3), (2) Web UI for PMs (months 4-6), (3) Export integration with doc platforms (months 7-9). The open-source maintainer audience is attractive but small; they're better served as evangelists than primary users. Key success metric: time from npm install to first completed session should be under 10 minutes for a developer who has read the README.
1.1.2.critic: The audience definition is too broad and internally contradictory. A 'TypeScript developer building LLM-powered applications' is a very specific persona — these are early adopters building with OpenAI/Anthropic APIs, not the mainstream developer population. Assuming they understand 'npm ecosystems and basic AI/ML concepts' may alienate the larger market of developers who build traditional CRUD apps and could benefit from structured specs. The claim that 'technical writers need structured input for generating documentation pipelines' is aspirational; most technical writers use Markdown in Git repos and would not adopt a 326-question tool for documentation. The framework's explanatory approach ('explains these concepts progressively through Series 1') assumes users will complete all 326 questions, but completion rates for long structured inputs are typically below 15%. The real audience is likely much narrower: technically sophisticated developers who are already bought into structured specification methodologies (like Behavior-Driven Development practitioners) and are looking for a more comprehensive framework. Marketing to a broader audience risks disappointing users who expect a simpler tool.

1.2.1.architect: SPACE can take for granted foundational software engineering concepts: module systems, async control flow, type systems, and data serialization. The output can assume familiarity with the TypeScript ecosystem (interfaces, generics, union types) since the entire codebase is TypeScript. However, several concepts must be introduced from scratch: the FrameworkDefinition structure (the 7-series hierarchy is SPACE-specific), the ArtifactDictionary pattern (a dynamic key-value store where keys are semantically meaningful and values carry provenance metadata), and the dependency graph model (how series consume artifacts from predecessor series). The JAD facilitation model should be referenced but not assumed — the system's progressive questioning approach borrows from JAD but operates differently. The OWL-style ontological modeling reference is aspirational; the system extracts entity definitions from free-text answers but does not implement formal reasoning. What must be explained from scratch: the concept of a 'probe' (a structured question designed to elicit specific information), the 'artifact' as a living document that evolves across series, and the snapshot mechanism for preserving intermediate state.
1.2.1.practitioner: The prior art SPACE can leverage includes: dependency graph implementations (topological sort in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts), state machine patterns for session lifecycle (created → in_progress → completed), and repository pattern for storage (src/storage/types.ts defines the StorageProvider interface). The practitioner should reference existing TypeScript patterns: discriminated unions for SpaceEvent types (already in types/index.ts), branded types for session/project IDs, and the builder pattern for ExportOptions. Concepts requiring explanation from scratch: the context_template interpolation system (how question text adapts based on prior artifacts), the artifact confidence scoring (0.0-1.0 scale in ArtifactValue), and the quality scoring dimensions in src/llm/quality-scorer.ts (completeness, specificity, consistency, actionability). The completeness-scorer in src/intelligence/ implements a custom scoring algorithm that doesn't follow standard heuristics — this needs API docs. The snapshot-manager.ts creates periodic checkpoints during sessions, which is an uncommon pattern in CLI tools that practitioners may not expect.
1.2.1.strategist: Prior art the market recognizes: ChatGPT for ad-hoc prompting, Jasper/Copy.ai for content generation templates, and Notion AI for document augmentation. SPACE differentiates by being specification-focused rather than content-focused. The concepts it must explain from scratch (probe-based elicitation, artifact dictionaries, series dependencies) are its unique value props and competitive moat — these are the innovations that justify a standalone tool rather than a ChatGPT plugin. The risk is that explaining these concepts requires significant documentation investment. The strategy should be: invest heavily in the first-session experience (guided walkthrough with pre-filled example answers) so users learn by doing rather than reading. The 'prior art' positioning matters for investor conversations: frame SPACE as 'requirements engineering meets prompt engineering' rather than 'a complex questionnaire tool.' The emerging area recognition is important — the tooling market for AI-assisted development is pre-Category, meaning the first well-positioned tool can define the category.
1.2.1.critic: The assumption that users understand 'CLI tool usage, npm, and TypeScript basics' is already a significant filter that excludes most software professionals. The real issue is that the 'foundational concepts' SPACE requires aren't just technical — they include an entire methodology (structured elicitation, progressive deepening, artifact dictionaries) that has no mainstream precedent. This means SPACE is simultaneously trying to introduce a new methodology AND build tooling for it, which is a much harder go-to-market challenge than building tooling for an established methodology. The JAD reference is problematic: Joint Application Development was popular in the 1990s enterprise space and is largely forgotten. Referencing it adds no value for the target audience. The OWL-style ontology claim should be dropped entirely — the system does simple key-value artifact extraction, not formal ontological reasoning. Being honest about what the system does (structured questioning with artifact extraction and multi-format export) is more compelling than dressing it up with academic terminology. The assumption that 'the artifact dictionary becomes a living knowledge base' is only true if users return to the tool repeatedly, which assumes a retention mechanism that doesn't exist in the current design.

1.2.2.architect: The mixed abstraction approach is architecturally sound because SPACE operates at multiple levels simultaneously: the question framework (abstract, declarative), the engine (concrete, imperative), and the LLM integration (probabilistic, contextual). Presenting the dependency graph as a structural diagram first grounds the reader in the system's topology, then concrete code examples from src/engine/question-router.ts demonstrate how the abstract graph is traversed at runtime. The key architectural insight is that the system has two distinct abstraction layers: (1) the framework definition layer (JSON files, immutable, purely declarative) and (2) the session/execution layer (TypeScript runtime, mutable state, imperative logic). The abstraction level should shift as the document progresses: Series 1 answers establish conceptual grounding (abstract), Series 2-3 build the entity model (semi-formal), and Series 4-7 specify implementation details (concrete). This mirrors the actual codebase structure where src/types/ is abstract, src/engine/ is semi-abstract, and src/cli/ is concrete.
1.2.2.practitioner: The concrete examples should ground each concept in actual code paths. For example, when explaining the dependency graph, show how src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts implements topological sort over the DependencyGraph type from src/types/index.ts. When explaining artifact extraction, show how src/data/artifact-mapping.ts transforms free-text AnswerEntry values into structured ArtifactValue objects. The session lifecycle can be demonstrated by walking through src/engine/session-manager.ts: session.create() → session.submitAnswer() → session.nextQuestion() → session.export(). Each code example should include the function signature, a brief usage pattern, and the relevant type contract. The engine's core loop (in src/engine/core.ts) is the most concrete demonstration: it shows how the system moves from question to question, checks dependencies, extracts artifacts, and tracks progress. Concrete error handling examples should reference src/engine/validator.ts patterns like ValidationResult and the error code conventions used in SpaceEvent.
1.2.2.strategist: The abstraction level decision directly impacts developer adoption speed. If SPACE starts too abstract (methodology-first), developers will lose interest before seeing working code. If it starts too concrete (install-and-run), they won't understand the 326-probe framework's value. The recommended approach for the web audience: lead with the output (a sample specification generated by SPACE) then work backward to the methodology. For the CLI audience: lead with the command (npx space init) and let the progressive questioning demonstrate the methodology in practice. The strategic document should maintain two parallel tracks: a 'quick start' (concrete, 5 minutes to first spec) and a 'deep dive' (abstract, comprehensive architecture explanation). Market data suggests developer tools with both tracks see 3x higher conversion than tools that only offer one. The output abstraction level should match the audience's decision-making needs: PMs need the output (what does a SPACE spec look like?), architects need the architecture (how does the system work?), and developers need the code (how do I implement this?).
1.2.2.critic: The mixed abstraction approach risks incoherence. If the document starts abstract and shifts to concrete without clear signposting, readers will be disoriented. The claim that it 'grounds each concept with concrete examples from the actual codebase' assumes the codebase is stable enough to reference — in an active development phase, code examples rot quickly. A more robust approach would be to keep the specification abstract and provide a separate 'implementation guide' with code examples that can be updated independently. The progressive deepening described ('Series 1 establishes grounding, Series 2-3 builds entities, Series 4-7 specifies details') sounds elegant but may not survive contact with real users who want to skip ahead. The abstraction level assumption also fails for the web audience: web users expect instant visual feedback, not progressive methodology revelation. The biggest flaw is assuming that one document format can serve both the architect (who wants diagrams) and the practitioner (who wants code). These are different documents for different audiences, and trying to serve both dilutes both.

1.3.1.architect: SPACE establishes a domain-specific vocabulary that must be used with absolute consistency across all interfaces — CLI output, web UI, exported specs, and documentation. Key terms that carry architectural significance: 'session' (a bounded execution context, not a user session), 'artifact' (derived structured data, not a build artifact), 'series' (a question group, not a data series), 'round' (a progressive step within a series), 'probe' (an elicitation question, not a network probe). The vocabulary follows the Adapter pattern — mapping general concepts to SPACE-specific terms. The notation conventions should follow JSON Schema patterns for the framework definition files and TypeScript conventions for the codebase. Terms to deliberately avoid: 'prompt' (confusing with LLM prompts — SPACE uses 'question' or 'probe'), 'model' (confusing with ML models — SPACE uses 'framework' or 'entity'), 'template' (confusing with HTML templates — SPACE uses 'context_template' for the specific field). The established standard is: all SPACE-specific terms are lowercase with underscores (snake_case), matching the JSON framework file convention.
1.3.1.practitioner: In the codebase, terminology is enforced through TypeScript types in src/types/index.ts. The interface names serve as vocabulary anchors: SessionState, ArtifactDictionary, FrameworkDefinition, QuestionContext. When implementing new features, developers must use these exact type names — not synonyms. The src/cli/tui.ts and web/ should display the same terminology to users. For example, the CLI shows 'Series 2: Ontological Characteristics' and the web UI must show the identical label. The artifact key naming convention (e.g., 'entity_list', 'domain_scope', 'tech_stack') should be documented in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts with JSDoc comments explaining each key's semantic meaning. When writing tests, test descriptions should use the canonical terminology: 'should complete round when all questions answered' not 'should finish step when all prompts done.' The context_template interpolation system uses {{artifact_key}} placeholders that reference the artifact dictionary — the syntax is Mustache-style (double curly braces) and should not be confused with TypeScript template literals.
1.3.1.strategist: The terminology choice directly impacts SEO, community building, and market positioning. 'Probe' is more distinctive than 'question' and creates a unique search identity — when users search 'SPACE probes' or 'elicitation probes,' the tool owns that keyword space. 'Artifact' is problematic because it collides with Maven/Gradle build artifacts in developer search results. Consider 'spec artifact' or 'design artifact' as a compound term to differentiate. The vocabulary decisions should be finalized before any public documentation is published — changing terminology after launch creates migration pain and community confusion. The established standards alignment matters for integration: if SPACE artifacts follow JSON Schema conventions, they can be consumed by tools like Postman, Swagger, and OpenAPI generators, which expands the addressable market. The deliberate avoidance of 'prompt' is strategically important — it positions SPACE as distinct from prompt engineering tools, which is correct because SPACE is a specification tool that happens to use LLMs, not a prompt engineering tool that happens to generate specs.
1.3.1.critic: The terminology enforcement is inconsistent across the existing codebase. The CLI in src/cli/tui.ts uses 'Question' in user-facing text, while the artifact system refers to 'probes.' The web UI (web/) likely has its own terminology choices. This inconsistency will confuse users who see different terms for the same concept across interfaces. The snake_case convention for artifact keys ('entity_list', 'domain_scope') is developer-friendly but not user-friendly — the web UI should present these as human-readable labels ('Entity List', 'Domain Scope') while maintaining the snake_case keys internally. The biggest vocabulary problem is 'session' — in web development, 'session' universally means 'user authentication state,' so using it for 'a run through the questionnaire' will cause confusion. A better term would be 'survey run' or 'spec run.' The deliberate avoidance of 'template' is undermined by the framework itself using context_template as a field name. The claim that terminology follows 'JSON Schema patterns' is aspirational — the framework JSON files use a custom format that doesn't conform to JSON Schema's vocabulary.

1.3.2.architect: The progressive complexity distribution follows the Layered Architecture pattern, where each layer builds on the previous one's abstractions. Layer 1 (Series 1) establishes the vocabulary and basic data model — FrameworkDefinition, SessionState. Layer 2 (Series 2-3) introduces the artifact extraction pipeline and dependency resolution. Layer 3 (Series 4-5) adds LLM integration and quality scoring. Layer 4 (Series 6-7) specifies export formats and deployment. This layering maps directly to the src/ directory structure: types/ → engine/ → llm/ → export/. The architectural benefit is that each layer can be understood, tested, and modified independently. The risk of this approach is that users who only complete Series 1-2 will have an incomplete mental model of the system's full capabilities. The mitigation is that each series' output (exported specification) should be independently useful, not just a stepping stone to the full specification.
1.3.2.practitioner: The progressive scaffolding should mirror the actual implementation order. In src/engine/core.ts, the core loop starts with the simplest case: load framework → display question → collect answer → extract artifacts → route to next question. Each subsequent file adds complexity: dependency-resolver.ts adds graph traversal, validator.ts adds answer quality checks, snapshot-manager.ts adds state persistence, session-manager.ts adds resume/abandon lifecycle. The implementation should follow this same progressive pattern in tests: first test the basic question-answer loop, then add dependency resolution, then add artifact extraction, then add LLM refinement. The complexity distribution in user-facing output (CLI and web) should match: the initial questions are simple and self-contained, later questions reference earlier artifacts ('Based on your earlier answer about [entity_list], which relationships exist between...'). The context_template field on each OpenEndedQuestion drives this progressive revelation — earlier questions have no context_template, later ones interpolate prior artifacts.
1.3.2.strategist: Progressive scaffolding is the right approach for developer tool adoption — it's the pattern used by successful tools like Vite (zero-config start, optional customization), Next.js (file-based routing, optional API routes), and Prisma (simple schema, optional migrations). The strategic benefit is a low barrier to entry (first question takes 30 seconds) with increasing depth (full specification takes 2-4 hours). The risk is that the 'progressive' part becomes 'prolonged' — if Series 1-2 feel like busywork before the interesting stuff arrives, users will abandon. The mitigation is to ensure each series produces immediately useful output: after Series 2, the user should have a usable entity list. After Series 4, they should have a working prototype prompt. The product strategy should market the 'minimum viable specification' (after Series 2-3, approximately 60 questions) as a complete product for simple projects, with Series 4-7 as optional depth for complex projects. This creates a natural upsell path from the free CLI (basic questions) to the web UI (full 326-probe experience with visualization).
1.3.2.critic: The progressive scaffolding assumption breaks down in practice because SPACE's 326 questions are front-loaded with methodology questions (Series 1: Domain & Audience, Assumptions & Abstraction) that most practitioners will find tedious. The 'simple to deep' progression assumes users are learning the methodology as they answer, but most developers just want to describe their project and get a spec — they don't want to first articulate their 'primary domain,' 'intended audience,' and 'foundational concepts.' A better approach would be to invert the progression: start with the concrete (what are you building? what entities does it have? how do they relate?) and derive the abstract (what domain is this? who is the audience?) as downstream inferences. The claim that 'each series' output should be independently useful' is aspirational — a specification that only covers domain/audience and entity discovery (Series 1-2) is not useful as a development spec. The complexity distribution also fails for the web UI: web users expect visual feedback (charts, progress bars, entity diagrams) which adds implementation complexity that the CLI doesn't face. The progressive model is a content architecture decision being presented as a UX decision, and these serve different masters.

2.1.1.architect: The primary entity model follows the Aggregate pattern from Domain-Driven Design. The Framework aggregate root contains Series, which contain Rounds, which contain Questions, which contain Choices — this is a strict containment hierarchy where child entities cannot exist without their parent. Session is the runtime aggregate root that accumulates Answers and the ArtifactDictionary. The dependency graph (DependencyGraph with DependencyNode and DependencyEdge) exists outside both aggregates, connecting Series definitions to their artifact dependencies. The Project aggregate wraps multiple Sessions, supporting the use case of iterating on a specification across sessions. Architecturally, the clean separation between FrameworkDefinition (read-only schema) and SessionState (mutable runtime) follows CQRS principles — the query side reads the framework, the command side writes answers and extracts artifacts. The entities should be modeled as immutable value objects within the Framework aggregate and as mutable entities within the Session aggregate.
2.1.1.practitioner: The entity list maps to TypeScript interfaces in src/types/index.ts. FrameworkDefinition → Framework, SeriesDefinition → Series, RoundDefinition → Round, OpenEndedQuestion → Question, MultiChoice → Choice. These are the 'definition' types (static, loaded from JSON). SessionMeta, AnswerEntry, ArtifactValue, ProgressState are the 'runtime' types (mutable, persisted to storage). The src/data/framework-loader.ts reads JSON files and produces FrameworkDefinition objects. The src/engine/question-router.ts traverses the framework's series/round/question hierarchy using the SeriesDefinition.rounds array. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys — this is the critical bridge between the definition layer and the runtime layer. When implementing new entity types, check if they belong in the definition layer (add to FrameworkDefinition side) or the runtime layer (add to SessionState side). The storage layer (src/storage/types.ts) defines how entities are serialized to SQLite or filesystem.
2.1.1.strategist: The entity model is the foundation for all product features. The Framework entity (the 326-question structure) is the primary intellectual property — it encodes the methodology that differentiates SPACE. The Session entity represents the user's work product — completed sessions are the output users value and share. The ArtifactDictionary is the bridge between input (answers) and output (specifications) — it's where AI augmentation adds the most value through extraction and refinement. The Project entity supports team use cases (multiple sessions for the same project, compare-and-merge workflows) that justify paid tiers. Product roadmap should prioritize: (1) Framework authoring tools (let users customize the 326 probes), (2) Session sharing (let team members see each other's answers), (3) Artifact visualization (entity relationship diagrams from the artifact dictionary). The entity model's clean separation between definition and runtime enables a marketplace where users can author and share custom frameworks — a significant revenue opportunity.
2.1.1.critic: The entity list has gaps. There's no 'User' or 'Respondent' entity — the system assumes a single user per session, but real-world use cases involve multiple stakeholders answering different questions. The 'Choice' entity (MultiChoice) conflates two different things: pre-authored follow-up choices (part of the framework definition) and user selections (part of the answer). The src/types/index.ts uses 'MultiChoice' for the definition side and 'multi_choice_id' in AnswerEntry for the selection, which is correct but the naming creates confusion. More critically, there's no 'Version' entity — when the framework is updated (new probes added, existing ones modified), there's no mechanism to track which version of the framework a session was created against, despite framework_version appearing as a string field. The entity model also lacks a 'Tag' or 'Label' entity for categorizing artifacts, which will be needed for the export layer to group related artifacts. The DependencyGraph being separate from the Framework entity is an architectural smell — it should be embedded within the Framework definition.

2.1.2.architect: Entity attributes follow the DDD value object pattern where identity is defined by the combination of key attributes rather than a surrogate ID. For FrameworkDefinition entities, the id field (series number, round number, question ID string) serves as a natural key derived from the hierarchy path. For SessionState entities, the id is a UUID assigned at creation time. The differentiation between entity types is driven by their attribute sets: SeriesDefinition has depends_on/consumes/provides (relationship metadata), RoundDefinition has focus (thematic grouping), OpenEndedQuestion has context_template (dynamic content), and MultiChoice has weight (selection influence). The attribute types follow a consistent convention: strings for display values, numbers for ordering/scoring, booleans for flags, arrays for collections, and Record types for key-value mappings. The ArtifactValue interface is notable for including confidence (0.0-1.0) and source_question_id — these provenance attributes enable the intelligence layer in src/intelligence/ to assess quality and traceability.
2.1.2.practitioner: Each entity's attributes map to specific implementation concerns. SessionMeta.status uses a TypeScript string literal union ('created' | 'in_progress' | 'completed' | 'abandoned') — this is a state machine pattern where transitions are managed by session-manager.ts. AnswerEntry includes edit_count and quality_score for the intelligence layer — these are updated by src/llm/quality-scorer.ts after each answer submission. ArtifactValue.value is typed as 'any', which is a deliberate flexibility trade-off — artifact values can be strings, arrays, objects, or primitives depending on the extraction logic in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts. The ProgressState entity tracks completed_rounds and completed_series as arrays of strings/numbers — these are denormalized for O(1) lookup during progress calculations in src/engine/progress.ts. The LLMMetadata entity tracks token usage per session, enabling cost monitoring — the total_tokens_used field is incremented by each LLM provider in src/llm/providers/.
2.1.2.strategist: The attribute design reveals product priorities. The quality_score on AnswerEntry suggests that answer quality matters — this enables a 'quality gate' feature where users cannot proceed to the next series until answers meet a threshold, which differentiates SPACE from simple questionnaire tools. The confidence field on ArtifactValue enables a 'low confidence' alert system that prompts users to refine vague answers. These intelligence features justify the premium pricing tier. The edit_count attribute suggests SPACE tracks iteration — this can power a 'revision history' feature that shows how specifications evolve. The framework_version field on SessionMeta enables backward compatibility — when SPACE releases a new framework version, users can still access sessions created with older versions. The lack of a 'priority' or 'importance' attribute on AnswerEntry is a product gap — not all 326 questions are equally important for every project, and a priority system would let users focus on the most impactful questions first.
2.1.2.critic: The ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any' is a significant type safety violation. While it provides flexibility, it means the artifact dictionary cannot be validated at compile time — a typo in a key like 'entity_lsit' instead of 'entity_list' won't be caught until runtime. A better approach would be a typed artifact registry where each known artifact key has a defined value type. The quality_score on AnswerEntry (0.0-1.0) is dangerously vague — what does a 0.7 quality score mean? Without dimension-specific scoring (the QualityResult interface in types/index.ts has completeness/specificity/consistency/actionability but this isn't used on AnswerEntry), the single score is meaningless. The edit_count attribute suggests a 'mutable answers' model, but the dependency graph assumes answers are stable once submitted — if a user edits a Series 1 answer after completing Series 3, downstream artifacts may become inconsistent. The framework_version field is a string with no schema — there's no mechanism to compare versions or detect incompatibilities. The ProgressState.completed_rounds being stored as string[] means progress tracking requires array scanning rather than a more efficient set or bitmap.

2.1.3.architect: Three natural categories emerge that map to architectural layers. Category 1 (Structural: Framework, Series, Round, Question, Choice) forms the schema layer — these entities are immutable, loaded from JSON, and define the system's shape. They follow the Decorator pattern where each level adds context to the level below. Category 2 (Runtime: Session, Answer, Artifact) forms the execution layer — these entities are mutable, persisted to storage, and track user progress. They follow the State pattern where Session's state determines which Questions are available. Category 3 (Output: Export, Project) forms the delivery layer — these entities represent consumable artifacts that the system produces. The classification also follows the Builder pattern: Structural entities are the blueprint, Runtime entities are the construction process, and Output entities are the finished product. The three categories have distinct persistence strategies: Structural entities are serialized as JSON files (immutable), Runtime entities are stored in SQLite (transactional), and Output entities are generated on-demand (ephemeral).
2.1.3.practitioner: The three categories map to src/ subdirectories. Category 1 (Structural) lives in src/data/ — the framework-loader.ts reads JSON files and produces FrameworkDefinition objects. Category 2 (Runtime) lives in src/engine/ and src/storage/ — the engine operates on SessionState, which is persisted by the StorageProvider. Category 3 (Output) lives in src/export/ — the exporters read SessionState and produce ExportResult objects. In practice, the boundaries between categories leak: the ArtifactDictionary (Runtime) is derived from Structural entities (Questions) via src/data/artifact-mapping.ts. The quality scoring in src/intelligence/ reads Runtime entities (Answers) and produces metadata about them. When implementing new features, determine which category the new entity belongs to by asking: (1) Is it loaded from JSON at startup? → Structural. (2) Is it created during a session? → Runtime. (3) Is it generated when the user requests output? → Output.
2.1.3.strategist: The three-category classification maps to three distinct product capabilities: (1) Framework authoring (customizing the 326 probes), (2) Session management (the interactive questioning experience), and (3) Export and delivery (specification output). Each category represents a different user value and monetization opportunity. Category 1 is the intellectual property — the methodology encoded in the 326 probes. A framework marketplace where users can author, share, and sell custom probe sets could be a revenue stream. Category 2 is the user experience — the guided questioning flow, progress tracking, and artifact extraction. This is where UX differentiation matters most. Category 3 is the output — the specification documents that users share with their teams. Export quality directly impacts word-of-mouth adoption. The product strategy should invest disproportionately in Category 2 (experience) because that's where users spend their time, while leveraging Category 1 (content) as the moat and Category 3 (output) as the viral mechanism.
2.1.3.critic: The three-category classification is neat but misses important cross-cutting concerns. The LLM integration layer (src/llm/) doesn't fit cleanly into any category — it operates on Runtime entities (Answers) using Structural entity context (Questions) to produce enhanced Runtime entities (refined Answers, extracted Artifacts). The Intelligence layer (src/intelligence/) similarly spans categories, reading Runtime entities and producing meta-information about them. The event system (SpaceEvent types in types/index.ts) is an orthogonal concern that cuts across all three categories. This categorization also creates a misleading implication that the layers are strictly sequential (define → run → export), when in reality the system supports iterative workflows where users run a session, export a partial spec, refine answers, and re-export. The 'distinct persistence strategies' claim (JSON files for Structural, SQLite for Runtime, on-demand for Output) is incorrect — the framework JSON files are actually compiled into the source code at build time, not loaded dynamically. This means customizing the framework requires rebuilding the tool, which undermines the 'framework authoring' product opportunity.

2.2.1.architect: The core-peripheral classification follows the concept of essential complexity from Fred Brooks' 'No Silver Bullet.' The 5 core entities (Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, Engine) represent the irreducible complexity of the system — remove any one and the system cannot function. The Engine is the orchestrator that coordinates between Framework (what to ask), Session (what has been answered), and Artifact (what has been extracted). The peripheral entities (Series, Round, Choice, Project, Export) are organizational or additive — they improve usability but the system could theoretically function with a flat list of questions, a simple answer store, and a single export format. The architectural implication is that the core 5 entities should receive the most rigorous type definitions, the most comprehensive test coverage, and the most careful change management. The peripheral entities can be refactored with lower risk.
2.2.1.practitioner: In the codebase, core entities are represented by the most referenced types. FrameworkDefinition is imported by src/data/framework-loader.ts, src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts, and src/engine/question-router.ts. SessionState is imported by src/engine/session-manager.ts, src/engine/core.ts, and all export formatters. QuestionContext is the primary input to the engine's core loop. ArtifactDictionary is consumed by src/data/artifact-mapping.ts, src/llm/artifact-synthesizer.ts, and every exporter. The Engine itself is the main orchestrator in src/engine/core.ts. Peripheral entities have more isolated usage: Series is only accessed through FrameworkDefinition.series, Round is accessed through Series.rounds, Choice is accessed through Question.follow_up_choices, Project is managed by src/storage/, and Export is the output of src/export/. When prioritizing bug fixes or refactoring, core entity issues should be addressed first because their failure cascades to all peripheral consumers.
2.2.1.strategist: The core-peripheral classification has direct product implications. Core entities represent the MVP — without Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, and Engine, there is no product. The minimum viable product ships with these 5 entities and minimal peripheral support (flat question list instead of Series/Round hierarchy, single JSON export instead of 6 formats). The peripheral entities are features that expand the addressable market: the Series/Round hierarchy (Series, Round) enables the 'progressive deepening' UX that appeals to structured thinkers. Multiple export formats (Export) enable integration with existing documentation pipelines. The Project entity enables team collaboration. Product roadmap should invest in core entities first (months 1-3 for CLI MVP), then expand peripheral entities to drive adoption: export formats (months 4-6 for developer adoption), project management (months 7-9 for team adoption), and custom frameworks (months 10-12 for platform play). The core-peripheral distinction also informs pricing: core features are free (OSS CLI), peripheral features are paid (web UI with team features, advanced exports).
2.2.1.critic: The 5-entity core is debatable. The Engine is not an entity — it's a service/controller that operates on entities. Including it in the 'core entity' list conflates the entity model with the service layer, which is an architectural smell. The true core entities are Framework, Session, Question, and Artifact. Engine, Series, Round, and Choice are structural or behavioral concerns, not entities. This misclassification could lead to poor design decisions, like giving Engine persistent state (it shouldn't — it's stateless and operates on SessionState). The claim that 'the system could function with a flat list of questions' understates the importance of the Series/Round structure — without it, the dependency graph cannot function, which means artifacts cannot be consumed by downstream questions. The Series/Round hierarchy is not peripheral; it's essential for the progressive specification methodology that defines SPACE. The peripheral classification of Project is also wrong — multi-session support (Project) is essential for any real-world usage where the first attempt is rarely the final specification.

2.2.2.architect: Moderate granularity is the correct architectural choice because SPACE's entity model serves two masters: the framework definition layer (which benefits from fine-grained entities for flexible question composition) and the session/execution layer (which benefits from coarse-grained entities for simpler state management). The splitting heuristic is: split when two concepts have distinct lifecycles, different relationships to other entities, or when conflating them would violate a business invariant. Following this heuristic: Session and Answer must be separate because a Session persists without Answers (empty session), but an Answer cannot exist without a Session. Question and Choice must be separate because Choices are part of the framework definition (read-only) while Answers to Choices are runtime state. Artifact and Answer must be separate because multiple Answers can produce a single Artifact (synthesized from multiple questions) and one Answer can produce multiple Artifacts.
2.2.2.practitioner: The granularity decision manifests in the TypeScript types. SessionState contains answers as Record<string, AnswerEntry> — answers are embedded in the session, not standalone entities in the storage layer. This means Answer's lifecycle is tied to Session's lifecycle (save session → save answers). FrameworkDefinition contains the question hierarchy as nested arrays (Series → Round → Question → Choice) — this embedding simplifies loading but means individual questions cannot be loaded independently. The ArtifactDictionary is also embedded in SessionState, not a separate entity. The src/storage/sqlite.ts implements separate tables for sessions, answers, and artifacts, but the API layer treats them as a single unit (save/load the entire SessionState). When implementing new features, check whether the new concept needs independent storage (→ make it a separate entity) or can be embedded (→ make it a field or nested type). The practical test: can you query it independently? Artifacts can be queried independently for quality scoring, which is why they have their own storage table.
2.2.2.strategist: The granularity decision impacts feature development velocity. Coarser entities (embedding answers in sessions) mean fewer database tables, simpler queries, and faster implementation. Finer-grained entities (separate answer table with relationships) enable more features (answer history, cross-session comparison, team annotations). The current moderate granularity is appropriate for MVP but will need refinement for the team collaboration feature. Specifically, the Answer entity will need to support: multiple annotations per answer (team members commenting), approval workflows (stakeholder sign-off on answers), and version history (tracking edits). These features require Answer to be a first-class entity with its own lifecycle, not an embedded field in Session. The product decision is when to make this transition — doing it before team features are needed wastes engineering effort, doing it after creates a painful migration. Recommendation: defer the Answer entity extraction until team features are on the roadmap.
2.2.2.critic: The 'moderate granularity' answer is a hedge that avoids committing to a clear position. The reality is that the current implementation has inconsistent granularity: FrameworkDefinition embeds Series/Round/Question/Choice as a deep hierarchy, but SessionState embeds Answers as a flat Record<string, AnswerEntry>. This inconsistency means framework questions can be navigated hierarchically (series → round → question), but answers cannot (you query by question_id, not by series/round/question path). The ArtifactDictionary is a flat Record<string, ArtifactValue> that conflates entity types — 'entity_list' (an array of entity names) and 'domain_scope' (a string description) have completely different value types but share the same dictionary. The 'four-entity-test' described in the existing answer (distinct lifecycle, unique relationships, different attributes, independent query) is too strict — it would keep Question and Choice as the same entity since they share the same lifecycle and can't be queried independently. The granularity problem is that SPACE's model tries to serve both a static definition (framework) and a dynamic execution (session) with overlapping but non-identical entity sets, creating confusion about where boundaries should be drawn.

2.2.3.architect: Entity relationships follow three patterns: composition (Framework owns Series, Series owns Round), reference (Answer references Question, Artifact references Question), and aggregation (Project contains Sessions). The shared attributes (id, created_at, updated_at) are universal value object fields that could be extracted into a base type. The differentiation follows the Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model for ArtifactValue, where the value attribute can hold any type and the key provides semantic meaning. Inheritance is minimal — there's no type hierarchy among entities, which is a deliberate design choice to keep the model flat and simple. The relationship between Framework entities (definition) and Session entities (runtime) is the most architecturally significant: they share the same keys (question IDs, series numbers) but have different lifecycles and storage strategies. This is the Foreign Key pattern where Answer.question_id references Question.id across the definition/runtime boundary.
2.2.3.practitioner: Shared attributes are implemented as base interfaces that concrete entities extend. The id field is typed as string (UUID for runtime entities, hierarchical string like '1.1.1' for definition entities). The created_at/updated_at fields use ISO 8601 strings (not Date objects) for serialization compatibility — this is enforced in src/types/index.ts. The relationship between Answer and Question is maintained by the question_id field in AnswerEntry, which must match a valid question ID in the framework definition. The src/engine/validator.ts checks this referential integrity when answers are submitted. The ArtifactValue.source_question_id provides the reverse reference — tracing artifacts back to their source questions. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys, which is the schema for the reference relationship. When implementing cross-referencing features, use the question ID as the canonical join key between definition and runtime entities.
2.2.3.strategist: The entity relationships reveal the product's data model for team features. The Project → Session → Answer hierarchy enables a 'project workspace' where multiple team members complete sessions independently, and their answers are compared and merged. The Answer → Question reference enables 'question assignment' where different team members answer different questions (the architect answers Series 3 questions, the PM answers Series 1 questions). The Artifact → Question provenance (source_question_id) enables 'answer traceability' where stakeholders can see which answers contributed to which specification sections. These team features justify the transition from free CLI to paid web platform. The relationship model also supports 'framework customization' where users modify the question set — the composition relationship (Framework → Series → Round → Question) would need to become a reference relationship to support user-authored questions. This is a major architectural change that should be planned for the platform roadmap.
2.2.3.critic: The entity relationship model has a significant flaw: it assumes a single framework version per project, but the relationship between Session.framework_version and FrameworkDefinition is implicit (matched by string comparison) rather than explicit (foreign key with constraint). If a framework is updated and a session was created with the old version, there's no mechanism to detect or handle the mismatch. The ArtifactValue derived_from field (string[]) claims to track multi-hop derivation chains, but the artifact extraction in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts doesn't populate this field — it's aspirational, not implemented. The shared attributes (id, created_at, updated_at) are defined inconsistently: SessionMeta has them, but ArtifactValue does not (it has source_question_id and last_updated but no id or created_at). This inconsistency means artifacts cannot be individually tracked, versioned, or deleted. The EAV pattern for ArtifactDictionary is a known anti-pattern that sacrifices query performance and type safety for flexibility — a typed artifact registry would be more maintainable.

2.3.1.architect: SPACE's boundaries are deliberately narrow, following the Single Responsibility Principle. In scope: the elicitation engine (asking questions, collecting answers), artifact extraction (deriving structured data from free-text), and specification generation (multi-format export). Out of scope: project management (task tracking, sprint planning), code generation (transforming specs into source code), team collaboration (multi-user editing, permissions), and deployment (hosting, scaling). The system boundary is enforced architecturally by the src/ directory structure: anything outside the 7 core modules (engine, storage, llm, export, cli, data, intelligence) is out of scope. The integration boundary is the LLM provider interface in src/llm/types.ts — SPACE defines what it needs from an LLM (completion, refinement, synthesis) but doesn't depend on specific provider implementations. The storage boundary is the StorageProvider interface in src/storage/types.ts — SPACE defines storage operations but doesn't mandate SQLite vs. filesystem vs. cloud.
2.3.1.practitioner: The boundary constraints manifest in implementation decisions. The CLI (src/cli/) is the primary interface; there's no HTTP API server (the web UI in web/ uses a minimal Express server for the local dev experience). The storage layer supports two backends: SQLite (src/storage/sqlite.ts) for production and filesystem (src/storage/filesystem.ts) for portability. The LLM providers (src/llm/providers/) implement a common LLMProvider interface, allowing runtime provider switching without code changes. Out-of-scope boundaries are enforced by what's NOT implemented: no WebSocket server for real-time collaboration, no database migration system for schema evolution, no authentication/authorization layer. The export layer (src/export/) is the system's output boundary — it produces ExportResult objects that are written to disk or returned to the caller. The src/intelligence/ module is an optional enhancement layer that can be disabled without affecting core functionality.
2.3.1.strategist: The narrow scope is a strategic strength for the CLI tool (focused, reliable, fast to ship) but a weakness for the web platform (limited features compared to competitors like Notion, Linear, or Miro). The boundary decisions should be revisited as the product evolves: team collaboration (in scope for paid tiers), project management integration (in scope for enterprise), and code generation (potentially in scope for AI-assisted development). The out-of-scope boundaries define the partnership ecosystem: SPACE can integrate with Jira (project management), GitHub (code generation), and Figma (design specs) through its export format, rather than trying to replace these tools. The strategic boundary to watch is the LLM provider interface — as new providers emerge (Groq, Together, Fireworks), SPACE must support them quickly to stay relevant. The storage boundary is less critical since SQLite is sufficient for individual use; team features would require cloud storage (PostgreSQL, MongoDB) which is currently out of scope.
2.3.1.critic: The boundary definitions are aspirational rather than enforced. The web/ directory contains a server.mjs that serves a React frontend — this is technically a web server, contradicting the 'no HTTP API' claim. The integration/ directory exists but is apparently empty or experimental, suggesting the boundary is porous. More critically, the system's boundaries don't address data privacy: SPACE collects detailed project specifications that may contain proprietary information, but there's no encryption at rest, no access control, and no data retention policy. The 'out of scope' list excludes team collaboration, but the Project entity (src/types/index.ts) explicitly supports multiple sessions — this is team collaboration at the data model level. The narrow scope claim also ignores the LLM integration: by sending answers to external LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.), SPACE is de facto sharing project information with third parties, which is a significant scope expansion that isn't acknowledged. The boundary between 'SPACE' and 'the framework JSON files' is also unclear — are the 326 probes part of the tool or part of the methodology? This distinction matters for licensing and customization.

2.3.2.architect: Three external actors interact with SPACE through well-defined interfaces. The Human Respondent interacts through the CLI (stdin/stdout) or Web UI (HTTP), providing free-text answers that the system cannot validate structurally (they're open-ended by design). The LLM Provider interacts through the LLMProvider interface (src/llm/types.ts), receiving completion/refinement requests and returning structured responses — this is an Adapter pattern that abstracts away provider-specific differences. The Storage Backend interacts through the StorageProvider interface (src/storage/types.ts), receiving CRUD operations and persisting state. The architectural boundary with each external actor is different: the Human boundary is user-interface (imprecise, needs validation), the LLM boundary is API (structured, needs error handling), and the Storage boundary is persistence (durable, needs transaction guarantees). The dependency-resolver in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts is the internal component most affected by external actors because it must handle the case where LLM-based artifact extraction fails and fall back to user-provided answers.
2.3.2.practitioner: The external actor interactions are implemented as follows. Human Respondent → CLI: src/cli/tui.ts uses inquirer for prompts, chalk for styled output, and readline for input. Human Respondent → Web: web/server.mjs serves React UI that communicates via REST endpoints. LLM Provider → SPACE: src/llm/factory.ts creates provider instances (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama) based on config, each implementing the same interface. The null-provider.ts and template-provider.ts are test fixtures that don't make real API calls. Storage Backend → SPACE: src/storage/sqlite.ts uses sql.js (WebAssembly SQLite) for browser-compatible storage, and src/storage/filesystem.ts uses Node.js fs module for CLI storage. Error handling for external actors follows the circuit breaker pattern: LLM failures trigger a fallback to the template provider, storage failures trigger in-memory state with a warning. The src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts creates periodic checkpoints so sessions can be recovered if an external actor fails mid-operation.
2.3.2.strategist: The external actor model reveals three partnership opportunities. The LLM Provider relationship is the most strategically valuable — partnerships with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google could provide API credits, co-marketing, or early access to new models. The Storage Backend relationship is less critical for individual use but becomes important for team features (cloud storage partnerships with Supabase, PlanetScale, or Turso). The Human Respondent relationship is the core product — the interactive questioning experience is the primary value delivery mechanism. The external actor boundaries also define the competitive landscape: SPACE competes with other tools that use the same LLM providers (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) and the same storage backends (SQLite, JSON files). Differentiation comes from SPACE's structured methodology (the 326 probes) rather than its technology stack. The strategic risk is LLM provider dependency — if OpenAI raises prices or degrades quality, SPACE's value proposition weakens. The Ollama integration (local models) partially mitigates this by offering an offline, cost-free alternative.
2.3.2.critic: The external actor model underserves the most critical external actor: the downstream consumer of SPACE's output. The specification generated by SPACE is consumed by developers, project managers, and AI coding tools — but there's no formal interface for these consumers. The ExportResult type (content, filename, mime_type, size_bytes) is too generic to be useful as an integration contract. A real integration would require a structured specification schema (JSON Schema, OpenAPI-style) that downstream tools can validate against. The LLM provider abstraction is also weaker than claimed — the null-provider and template-provider are test doubles, not production fallbacks. If the real LLM provider fails, the system's artifact extraction quality drops significantly. The Storage Backend abstraction is unnecessary complexity for a CLI tool — SQLite is sufficient and the filesystem backend adds maintenance burden without clear user value. The most concerning external actor gap is the lack of a webhook or event system for triggering downstream workflows when a specification is completed.

2.3.3.architect: Each entity follows a well-defined state machine pattern. Session: created → in_progress → completed/abandoned (managed by session-manager.ts). Artifact: extracted → refined → finalized (managed by artifact-synthesizer.ts). The lifecycle transitions are guarded by business rules: a Session can only transition from created to in_progress when the first question is answered; from in_progress to completed when all required questions are answered; from in_progress to abandoned when the user explicitly cancels. The Framework entity has no lifecycle — it's immutable and loaded once at startup. The Question entity has an implicit lifecycle within a session: available → displayed → answered → locked (once answered, the question cannot be re-answered without editing the session). The Snapshot entity is create-only (no updates or deletes) — it's a write-ahead log entry that preserves session state at specific checkpoints. The export lifecycle is: generated → delivered (written to disk or returned to caller).
2.3.3.practitioner: The session lifecycle is implemented in src/engine/session-manager.ts with these key methods: create() (initializes SessionMeta with status='created'), submitAnswer() (transitions to in_progress, updates progress), complete() (transitions to completed, triggers final artifact synthesis), abandon() (transitions to abandoned, saves partial state). The status field uses TypeScript string literal types for compile-time safety. The artifact lifecycle is implicit in src/llm/artifact-synthesizer.ts: extract() creates ArtifactValue from answer text, refine() updates the value with LLM-enhanced content, and the confidence score increases as the artifact matures. The snapshot lifecycle in src/engine/snapshot-manager.ts is simple: create() is called at round/series boundaries and on-demand via the manual trigger. Snapshots are immutable — they're never updated or deleted. The export lifecycle is stateless: generate() in each formatter produces an ExportResult that is immediately written to disk.
2.3.3.strategist: The entity lifecycles reveal product opportunities. The Session lifecycle's 'abandoned' state is a retention metric — how many sessions are abandoned, and at which series? If most sessions are abandoned in Series 1 (methodology questions), the onboarding experience needs redesign. The Artifact lifecycle's 'refined' state enables a 'before/after' comparison feature that demonstrates LLM value — show users the raw artifact vs. the refined artifact to justify the LLM integration cost. The Snapshot lifecycle (create-only) enables a 'timeline' feature where users can browse their session's history and revert to any checkpoint — this is a compelling UX feature for the web platform. The export lifecycle being stateless means exports can be regenerated on-demand, which enables a 'live preview' feature where users see the specification update in real-time as they answer questions. The lifecycle metrics (time in each state, transition counts, abandonment rates) should be tracked for product analytics to identify friction points.
2.3.3.critic: The lifecycle model has gaps. The Session lifecycle allows 'abandoned' as a terminal state, but there's no mechanism to 'resume' an abandoned session — the status field doesn't include a 'resumed' state. In practice, users will want to abandon and later resume sessions, which requires either a new state ('paused') or a convention (abandoned sessions can be resumed by setting status back to in_progress). The Artifact lifecycle claims 'refined' as a state, but ArtifactValue has no status field — refinement is tracked implicitly by the confidence score and last_updated timestamp. This means you can't query 'all finalized artifacts' without inferring the state from other fields. The Snapshot lifecycle being immutable is correct for data integrity but problematic for storage — if a user creates many snapshots (every question), the storage grows unboundedly with no garbage collection mechanism. The export lifecycle being 'delivered' doesn't account for the case where the user requests an export but doesn't have write permissions to the output directory — the ExportResult is generated but never persisted, creating a ghost export.

2.4.1.architect: The entity model is comprehensive for the current scope but has three notable gaps. First, there's no 'User' or 'Respondent' entity — the system assumes a single user per session, tracked implicitly by the session creator. This prevents multi-stakeholder workflows where different team members answer different questions. Second, there's no 'Version' entity for framework evolution — when the 326-probe framework is updated, sessions created with the old version may reference artifacts that no longer exist. The framework_version string field exists but there's no version comparison or migration logic. Third, there's no 'Annotation' entity for in-context commentary — users may want to add notes to their answers ('I'm not sure about this, need to check with the architect') without modifying the answer text itself. These gaps are acceptable for MVP but will become blockers as the product matures.
2.4.1.practitioner: The missing entities would manifest as implementation challenges. A User entity would require adding user_id fields to Session, Answer, and Artifact, plus authentication logic in the CLI and web UI. The framework versioning issue is already partially addressed by the framework_version field in SessionMeta, but src/data/framework-loader.ts doesn't validate version compatibility — it loads whatever framework file is present. A practical workaround is to version the framework JSON files (framework-v1.json, framework-v2.json) and let the loader pick the matching version. The Annotation entity would be a new ArtifactDictionary entry type or a parallel annotation store. In the current implementation, users can add notes in the answer text field, but these notes pollute the answer and aren't machine-parseable. The src/types/index.ts AnswerEntry type could be extended with an optional notes: string[] field for MVP annotation support.
2.4.1.strategist: The missing entities represent future product features. The User entity is required for team features (multi-user sessions, role-based question assignment, answer approval workflows). The Version entity is required for the framework marketplace (versioned frameworks, upgrade migrations, backward compatibility). The Annotation entity is required for collaborative workflows (comments, questions, flags on answers). These are not gaps in the MVP — they're features in the product roadmap. The strategic question is when to add them. The User entity should be added when team features are on the roadmap (likely after CLI MVP proves demand). The Version entity should be added when the framework marketplace launches (platform phase). The Annotation entity can be approximated using the existing AnswerEntry.edit_count and answer text field for now, with a proper implementation when collaborative features ship. The gap analysis is useful for roadmap planning but should not delay the current sprint.
2.4.1.critic: The claim that 'no major entity gaps exist' is premature. The most significant missing entity is the 'Template' — a reusable specification template that users can start from instead of answering all 326 questions. The existing system forces every user through the same exhaustive process, which is why completion rates will be low. A Template entity would allow sharing 'starter specifications' that pre-fill common answers, drastically reducing friction. The second missing entity is 'Metric' — there's no way to define custom quality metrics beyond the fixed four dimensions (completeness, specificity, consistency, actionability). Different domains need different quality criteria. The third gap is the lack of a 'Constraint' entity — business rules and invariants are discussed in the answers but not modeled as first-class objects that can be validated, versioned, and exported. The 'no gaps' assessment reflects the current narrow scope (single-user CLI tool) but fails to anticipate the natural expansion to collaborative, customizable, and extensible use cases.

2.4.2.architect: The entity boundaries are clean and well-motivated based on the four-entity-test. However, there are three boundary cases worth examining. First, MultiChoice vs. Answer — a selected choice is semantically part of the answer, but in the model they're separate (MultiChoice is a framework entity, the selection is an AnswerEntry field). This separation is correct because the choice options are defined by the framework (immutable) while the selection is user input (mutable). Second, Artifact vs. Answer — an artifact is derived from one or more answers, but could be modeled as a specialized answer. The separation is justified because artifacts have different attributes (confidence, derived_from) and different lifecycle (extracted → refined → finalized vs. submitted → edited). Third, Export vs. Artifact — both are 'outputs' of the system, but exports are formatted representations of the session state while artifacts are intermediate structured data. The merge question doesn't apply because they serve different consumers (humans read exports, the engine consumes artifacts).
2.4.2.practitioner: The boundary verification passes in the codebase: each entity has a dedicated interface in src/types/index.ts, a dedicated storage representation in src/storage/sqlite.ts (separate tables for sessions, answers, artifacts), and a dedicated creation/management module (session-manager.ts for Session, artifact-synthesizer.ts for Artifact, export formatters for Export). The boundary between Series/Round and Question is enforced by the framework JSON structure — questions cannot exist outside their parent round, which cannot exist outside its parent series. The only boundary case I'd flag for practitioners: the 'context_template' field on OpenEndedQuestion is part of the Question entity but conceptually belongs to the template/interpolation system. If template logic becomes more complex (conditional sections, loops), this field should be extracted into a separate Template entity. Currently it's simple enough to keep inline.
2.4.2.strategist: The entity boundary decisions are correct for the current product scope and should not change. Merging entities would reduce feature flexibility; splitting entities would increase complexity without clear user value. The boundary validation ('four-entity-test') is a useful framework for evaluating future entity additions — any new entity must pass all four criteria. The strategic risk is not wrong boundaries but missing boundaries: the system doesn't clearly separate 'core product features' (free, OSS) from 'premium features' (paid, web-only) at the entity level. For example, ArtifactDictionary is a core entity but the LLM refinement of artifacts is a premium feature. This means the OSS CLI includes premium entity types that it can't fully utilize. A cleaner boundary would separate the entity model into 'core schema' (always present) and 'extended schema' (requires premium features). This enables a cleaner free/paid tier separation.
2.4.2.critic: The entity boundary verification is circular — it validates that current boundaries are consistent with current usage, but doesn't test whether better boundaries exist. The Round entity is the weakest link: it's primarily a grouping mechanism for questions within a series, with the 'focus' attribute as its only unique property. The focus string could be a field on Question instead, eliminating the Round entity entirely. This would simplify the hierarchy from 5 levels (Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice) to 4 levels (Framework → Series → Question → Choice). The 'focus' grouping could be achieved through question tags or metadata rather than a structural entity. The cost of removing Round would be minimal (update framework JSON structure, update loaders) but the benefit is a simpler mental model. Similarly, the 'depends_on' field on SeriesDefinition duplicates information that could be derived from the DependencyGraph — having both creates a consistency risk where the two representations diverge.

2.4.3.architect: Key constraints fall into three categories. Structural constraints (enforced at framework load time): Framework contains exactly 7 Series, each Series contains 3-5 Rounds, each Round contains 2-5 Questions, each Question contains 3-5 Choices. These are hardcoded in the framework JSON and validated by src/data/framework-loader.ts. Runtime constraints (enforced during session execution): each Question can be answered at most once per Session, dependencies must be satisfied before a Series is unlocked, and the ArtifactDictionary must contain all required artifacts before export. These are enforced by src/engine/validator.ts. Data integrity constraints (enforced at storage time): Answer.question_id must reference a valid question, Artifact.source_question_id must reference a valid question, and Session.framework_version must match the loaded framework version. These are enforced by the StorageProvider implementation. The most critical invariant is dependency satisfaction: a Series cannot be started until all its predecessor Series have been completed and their artifacts extracted.
2.4.3.practitioner: The constraints are implemented across multiple files. The framework structural constraints are validated in src/data/framework-loader.ts during initialization — if the JSON file doesn't match the expected structure, the loader throws a ValidationError with specific field paths. The runtime constraints are enforced in src/engine/validator.ts, which checks: (1) answer uniqueness per question (prevents duplicate submissions), (2) dependency satisfaction (checks ProgressState.completed_series against DependencyGraph.edges), and (3) artifact completeness (checks required artifacts exist before export). The data integrity constraints are enforced by TypeScript types at compile time (question_id is typed as string) and by the storage layer at write time (SQLite foreign key constraints if enabled, or application-level checks). The src/engine/question-router.ts enforces the dependency constraint by filtering available questions based on ProgressState.blocked_on, which lists question IDs whose dependencies are not yet satisfied.
2.4.3.strategist: The constraint system has product implications. The structural constraints (7 series, 3-5 rounds, etc.) are fixed by the framework definition — changing these requires updating the JSON files and potentially the code that validates them. This rigidity is acceptable for the v1 methodology but limits framework customization. The runtime constraints (dependency satisfaction, answer uniqueness) are the 'progressive deepening' mechanism that ensures users answer questions in the right order — this is a core product feature that prevents incomplete or inconsistent specifications. The data integrity constraints are essential for data reliability — without them, corrupted sessions could produce invalid specifications. The strategic constraint to highlight is the dependency satisfaction rule: it forces users to complete earlier series before starting later ones, which creates natural checkpoints for the 'minimum viable specification' feature. If a user completes Series 1-3, they should be able to export a useful partial specification even if Series 4-7 are incomplete.
2.4.3.critic: The constraint system has weaknesses. The structural constraints (exactly 7 series, 3-5 rounds) are enforced by convention, not by code — if someone manually edits the framework JSON to add an 8th series, the system may partially work or fail unpredictably. The runtime dependency constraint is too rigid: it prevents users from answering later questions even when they have the knowledge, forcing them through the full progression. A better approach would be to allow 'preview mode' where users can see and partially answer any question, with a 'validation mode' that checks completeness before export. The data integrity constraints are incomplete: there's no validation that ArtifactValue.confidence is between 0 and 1, no validation that AnswerEntry.quality_score matches the QualityResult dimensions, and no validation that the artifact dictionary keys follow a naming convention. The 'export must have all required artifacts' constraint is enforced by src/export/ but the error message is unclear — users need to know exactly which artifacts are missing and which questions produce them.

2.5.1.architect: The edge cases follow the robustness principle (be conservative in what you accept, liberal in what you send). Empty sessions are handled by allowing SessionMeta to exist with zero answers — the progress tracking calculates completion_pct as 0.0 and the export layer generates a skeleton specification with placeholder sections. Corrupted sessions are handled by the snapshot-manager.ts creating periodic checkpoints — if the current session state is corrupted, the most recent valid snapshot can be restored. Concurrent access is addressed by the single-writer model: only one process (CLI or web) modifies a session at a time, enforced by file locking in the filesystem backend.
