The dependency cycle edge case is prevented by the framework definition being a validated DAG — the dependency-resolver.ts performs a topological sort at startup and throws if a cycle is detected. The LLM failure edge case triggers a fallback to template-based artifact extraction (src/llm/providers/template-provider.ts).
2.5.1.practitioner: The edge case handling is implemented across several modules. Empty session: session-manager.ts allows create() without any answers; progress.ts calculates 0% completion. Corrupted session: snapshot-manager.ts creates checkpoints at round/series boundaries; on session load, if the state is corrupted, the system offers to restore from the latest snapshot. File locking: the filesystem storage backend uses lockfile (or similar) to prevent concurrent writes. LLM failure: src/llm/factory.ts wraps provider creation in try/catch and falls back to template-provider. Framework validation: src/data/framework-loader.ts checks the dependency graph for cycles using Kahn's algorithm. Framework version mismatch: currently not validated (a gap) — adding a version check in the loader would prevent loading sessions created with incompatible framework versions. The error handling convention in src/engine/ uses the SpaceEvent error type with a code and message, where codes follow the pattern 'ERROR_CATEGORY_SPECIFIC'.
2.5.1.strategist: Edge case handling directly impacts user trust and retention. An empty session that's handled gracefully (offering to restart or showing what would have been generated) builds confidence that the system is robust. A corrupted session that can be restored from a snapshot demonstrates reliability. The concurrent access prevention (single-writer model) is appropriate for individual use but becomes a blocker for team features — the product roadmap must plan for concurrent access (optimistic locking, conflict resolution) before multi-user support. The LLM failure fallback is critical for reliability: if the LLM is unavailable, the system should still produce a useful (if less refined) specification. The strategic edge case is 'partial specification export' — the current system likely requires all questions to be answered before export, but users will want to export after completing only part of the framework. This is the highest-value edge case to handle because it directly affects the 'time to first value' metric.
2.5.1.critic: The edge case analysis is incomplete. The most critical missing edge case is 'answer quality degradation' — what happens when a user gives intentionally bad or nonsensical answers? The artifact extraction will produce garbage artifacts, the quality scorer will flag them, but the system doesn't have a mechanism to block low-quality answers or force refinement. Another missing edge case: 'framework update during active session' — if the framework JSON is updated while a session is in progress, the session may reference questions that no longer exist. The concurrent access model ('single-writer') is described but not enforced — there's no file locking implementation in the codebase, just the assumption that users won't run two CLI instances simultaneously. The LLM fallback to 'template-provider' is a poor fallback because the template provider produces generic, unhelpful artifacts — a better fallback would be to skip artifact extraction for that question and flag it for manual review. The snapshot restoration claim is aspirational — the snapshot-manager creates snapshots but there's no UI or CLI command to restore from a snapshot.

2.5.2.architect: The composition hierarchy is a strict containment tree, which is the simplest and most predictable composition pattern. Framework → Series → Round → Question → Choice follows the Composite pattern where each level contains its children as arrays. This is appropriate because the containment is permanent — a Question always belongs to the same Round, a Round always belongs to the same Series. The cross-cutting dependency relationships exist outside this containment tree: Series A can depend on artifacts from Series B without containing or being contained by it. This is the Observer pattern where downstream series 'observe' artifact changes from upstream series. The aggregate roots are Framework (for definition data) and Project (for runtime data). All other entities are reachable through these roots, which simplifies serialization (save root → save all children) and deserialization (load root → load all children). The ArtifactDictionary is a flat key-value map that doesn't participate in the containment hierarchy — it's a value object owned by Session.
2.5.2.practitioner: The composition is implemented through nested array structures in TypeScript. FrameworkDefinition contains series: SeriesDefinition[], which contains rounds: RoundDefinition[], which contains open_ended: OpenEndedQuestion[], which contains follow_up_choices: MultiChoice[]. Loading is recursive: src/data/framework-loader.ts loads the entire JSON file into a single FrameworkDefinition object. Traversal uses nested iteration: the question-router.ts iterates through series → rounds → questions to find the next available question. The artifact dictionary is stored as Record<string, ArtifactValue> in SessionState, which is a flat map — no nested composition. The src/storage/sqlite.ts normalizes this hierarchy into separate tables (frameworks, series, rounds, questions, choices) for efficient querying, but the application layer works with the nested structure. The serialization format in ProjectArchive nests sessions as an array under the project, maintaining the containment relationship.
2.5.2.strategist: The composition hierarchy maps to product features. The strict containment tree enables 'series-level progress' — users can see completion by series (60% of Series 3 done, 0% of Series 4) and make informed decisions about where to focus. The cross-cutting dependency relationships enable 'smart question routing' — the system can skip questions whose dependencies are already satisfied by prior answers, reducing the effective question count from 326 to perhaps 200-250 for any given project. The flat artifact dictionary enables 'artifact visualization' — since artifacts are keyed by semantic names (not nested in a hierarchy), they can be displayed as a dashboard showing the current specification state. The aggregate root pattern (Framework and Project as roots) enables 'project templates' — a completed project can be cloned as a template for new projects, carrying all its sessions and artifacts. The product should highlight the composition hierarchy in the UI — a tree view showing the 7 series, their rounds, and questions gives users a sense of the methodology's scope.
2.5.2.critic: The strict containment hierarchy is overly rigid for a tool that aims to be flexible. Real-world projects don't always fit neatly into 7 predefined series — some projects need more domain questions and fewer technical questions. The containment hierarchy prevents users from reordering, merging, or skipping series. The cross-cutting dependency relationships are described but the DependencyGraph in src/types/index.ts uses a separate node/edge structure that duplicates information already encoded in the series' depends_on, consumes, and provides fields. This duplication creates a consistency risk — if the depends_on array and the DependencyGraph edges disagree, the system may behave unpredictably. The artifact dictionary being flat is a limitation — as the number of artifacts grows (potentially 100+), the flat structure becomes unwieldy. A hierarchical artifact organization (grouping artifacts by series or by entity type) would improve navigability. The aggregate root pattern assumes the entire project is loaded at once, which won't scale for projects with many sessions.

2.5.3.architect: The cardinality model follows a clean containment pattern with two notable exceptions. The dominant pattern is 1:N containment (Framework→Series, Series→Round, Round→Question, Question→Choice) with fixed cardinality bounds (7 series, 3-5 rounds, etc.). This is architecturally simple and enables efficient serialization. The many-to-one reference pattern (Answer→Question, Artifact→Question) represents the data flow from definition to runtime. The many-to-many pattern in the dependency graph (Series depends on multiple Series, Series provides to multiple Series) creates the DAG that governs question ordering. The optional relationships are significant: Session→Answer is 1:0..N because a session can exist before any answers are recorded; Session→Artifact is 1:0..N because artifacts are derived from answers and may not exist yet; Export→Session is N:1 because multiple export formats can be generated from one session. These optional cardinalities require null-checking in the implementation.
2.5.3.practitioner: The cardinality constraints are enforced at multiple layers. Framework→Series: 1:7 is hardcoded in the framework JSON files and validated by src/data/framework-loader.ts (checks series.length === 7). Series→Round: 1:3..5 is validated by the loader (checks each series has 3-5 rounds). Round→Question: 1:2..5 is validated similarly. Session→Answer: 1:0..326 is managed by the question-router.ts which tracks answered question IDs in ProgressState. The many-to-one references (Answer→Question) are maintained by the question_id field in AnswerEntry — the validator checks this against the framework's question IDs. The many-to-many dependency graph is stored in DependencyGraph with nodes (series_id → name, provides) and edges (from, to, artifacts). The optional relationships require defensive coding: when iterating artifacts, check if the artifact dictionary is empty; when generating exports, handle the case where no answers exist. The TypeScript types enforce optionality through optional fields (multi_choice_id?: string) and nullable types.
2.5.3.strategist: The cardinality model has product implications for pricing and scalability. The fixed 1:7 series cardinality means every SPACE project has the same structural complexity — this is good for consistent user experience but bad for projects that need fewer or more series. A 'lite' version (3 series, ~100 questions) would expand the addressable market to simpler projects. The Session→Answer cardinality of 0..326 means the system handles both quick explorations (answer 10 questions, get a draft spec) and comprehensive specifications (answer all 326 questions, get a complete spec). This flexibility supports multiple pricing tiers: free tier (first 50 answers), pro tier (unlimited answers with LLM refinement). The Export→Session N:1 cardinality enables 'export bundles' — a single session can produce JSON + Markdown + HTML + Prompt exports simultaneously, which is a premium feature. The dependency graph's many-to-many cardinality is the engine's competitive advantage — it enables intelligent question routing that no other tool offers.
2.5.3.critic: The cardinality model has issues that will surface as the product matures. The fixed 1:7 series cardinality is the most problematic — it assumes every project needs all 7 series, but many projects will only need 3-4. The system should support variable series counts, which means the '7' should be a derived value from the framework definition, not a hardcoded constant. The 0..326 Session→Answer cardinality is technically correct but misleading — it implies all 326 answers are equally required, when in practice some questions are conditional or optional. The dependency graph's many-to-many cardinality creates O(N²) worst-case complexity for topological sorting, though with only 7 series this is negligible. The most concerning cardinality issue is Artifact→Question: the many-to-one claim is incorrect for derived artifacts that are synthesized from multiple questions. The ArtifactValue type supports derived_from: string[] which implies many-to-many, contradicting the stated many-to-one. This inconsistency between the stated model and the actual implementation creates confusion for anyone trying to reason about the data model.
